## The problem

Support forwards a ticket: a user's password reset email never arrives. You look her up by email and get **two rows back**. Same email, two different ids, `created_at` values 400 milliseconds apart. One row has all of her tasks. The other is empty, and it is the one the reset flow found first.

Here is what happened. Signup was a POST behind a spinner. The network stalled, she tapped the button again, and your React Native app fired the request twice. The endpoint did the reasonable thing: select by email, see nothing, insert. Both requests ran that check before either insert landed. Both saw nothing. Both inserted. The check was correct and still useless, because it was application code asserting a fact that belongs to the storage. One phrase in the table definition would have made the second insert fail loudly instead of succeed quietly: `email text NOT NULL UNIQUE`.

## The idea

A table is a list screen with the pixels removed. Rows are the items, columns are the fields, and the column types are a type system that runs at write time instead of at compile time.

That last part is the whole point. TypeScript checks *your code*, before it runs, and only your code. A constraint checks *the data*, as it is written, for every writer forever: your API, a teammate's admin script, a migration, you pasting SQL into a dashboard at 1am. Anything enforced only in TypeScript is a promise. Anything in the schema is a guarantee.

Four words, precisely: a **table** is the collection, a **row** is one record, a **column** is one typed field, and a **primary key** is the value that identifies a row for the rest of its life.

## In practice

Here is a table with every kind of constraint you will use daily.

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email      text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  full_name  text,
  plan       text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'free' CHECK (plan IN ('free', 'pro', 'team')),
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
```

Read it as five decisions, not five lines. `id` is generated by the database, so no two writers can collide. `email` cannot be missing and cannot repeat. `full_name` is allowed to be absent, which is a product statement. `plan` has a default and a closed set of legal values. `created_at` is filled in by the database, not by whichever client happened to have a wrong clock.

The type choices matter more than they look:

| Instead of | Use | Because |
|---|---|---|
| `varchar(255)` | `text` | In Postgres they perform identically. `varchar(n)` is a length check hidden inside a type. If you need a cap, write `CHECK (length(title) <= 500)` so the rule is visible. |
| `timestamp` | `timestamptz` | `timestamp` has no timezone. It stores 09:00 and forgets whose 09:00. `timestamptz` stores an instant in UTC and renders it in the caller's zone. Your users are not all in one zone and neither are your servers. |
| auto-increment integer | `uuid` | Sequential ids leak volume and invite guessing your neighbour's row. UUIDs can also be generated on the device, which matters for offline-first mobile. |
| `float` for money | `numeric(12,2)` or integer cents | Floats are binary approximations. This will get its own module when you build the marketplace, but start the habit now. |

Then the four verbs. `INSERT` with `RETURNING` gives you the generated row back in one round trip, which is exactly what your RN client needs after a create.

```sql
INSERT INTO users (email, full_name)
VALUES ('aswin@example.com', 'Aswin R')
RETURNING id, created_at;
```

`SELECT` names the columns you actually need. `SELECT *` on a wide table ships bytes over the wire that no screen renders.

```sql
SELECT id, email, plan
FROM users
WHERE plan = 'pro'
  AND created_at >= now() - interval '30 days';
```

`UPDATE` and `DELETE` both take a `WHERE`, and the `WHERE` is the only thing between you and the whole table.

```sql
UPDATE users SET plan = 'pro' WHERE id = 'a1b2...' RETURNING plan;

DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 'a1b2...';
```

Run the `SELECT` version of the filter first, count the rows, then swap `SELECT` for `UPDATE`. Every experienced backend engineer does this, and it is because of the one time they did not.

## In your world

On day 12 you write `supabase/migrations/001_create_categories_and_tasks.sql` in `task-manager-api`, and it is exactly this shape: `uuid` primary keys with `gen_random_uuid()`, `timestamptz` for `created_at` and `updated_at`, `title text NOT NULL`, and `priority smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (priority BETWEEN 0 AND 3)`. That `CHECK` will still be there when your Zod schema has a bug, which is the whole argument for it.

Your work backend adds one layer of confusion worth naming now. It defines tables twice: once as a Drizzle schema file in TypeScript, and once as a SQL migration. The TypeScript file is how your code talks about the table. The migration is what actually changed the database. When those two disagree, the database wins and your types lie, which is why a schema change there is always a two-sided change.

## Watch out

- `NULL` is not a value, it is the absence of one, and it is not equal to anything including itself. `WHERE category_id = NULL` returns zero rows, always. You want `IS NULL`.
- `UNIQUE` permits many `NULL`s, because no two unknowns are known to be equal. A nullable unique column does not mean "at most one row".
- A `DEFAULT` only applies when the column is omitted from the insert. Send an explicit `null` and you get `null`, or an error if the column is `NOT NULL`.
- Constraints reject the whole statement. That is a feature: a failed insert is a 400 you can handle, while a bad row is a bug you find in six months.
tasks: Install Postgres locally and get a scratch database: `brew install postgresql@17`, `brew services start postgresql@17`, `createdb sqlplay`, then `psql sqlplay`.
Type out the `users` table above by hand (no copy-paste), then run `\d users` in psql and read back every constraint Postgres reports.
Insert the same email twice and read the exact error message and error code Postgres returns. Write the message down; you will map it to a 409 response later.
Insert a row with `plan` set to 'enterprise' and watch the CHECK constraint reject it. Then insert with `plan` omitted and confirm the default landed.
Run `SELECT * FROM users WHERE full_name = NULL;` on a table that has rows with a null name, get zero results, then fix it with `IS NULL` and explain out loud why the first one was wrong.

Add a second table `notes(id, user_id, body, created_at)` with no constraints at all, insert deliberately garbage rows (empty body, made-up user_id), then rewrite the table with the constraints that would have stopped each one.

quiz.q: Two concurrent signup requests both check `SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = $1`, both find nothing, and both insert. What actually prevents the duplicate?
options: Wrapping the check and the insert in a try/catch
A `UNIQUE` constraint on the email column
Checking again immediately after the insert
Rate limiting the signup endpoint
quiz.explain: Only the database can settle a question about the whole table at write time. A check-then-insert in application code has a gap between the two statements, and concurrency lives in that gap. The unique constraint makes the second insert fail with an error you can turn into a 409.

quiz.q: Why `timestamptz` rather than `timestamp` for a `created_at` column?
options: `timestamptz` is smaller on disk
`timestamp` cannot store sub-second precision
`timestamptz` stores an absolute instant in UTC and renders it in the caller's timezone; `timestamp` stores a wall-clock reading with no zone attached
`timestamptz` is required for indexes on date columns
quiz.explain: A plain `timestamp` records 09:00 without recording whose 09:00 it was, so the value changes meaning depending on who reads it. `timestamptz` records the instant, which is what "when did this happen" actually means.

quiz.q: A `status` column is `text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'`. A client sends an explicit `null` for it. What happens?
options: The default 'pending' is used, because the value was null
The insert fails, because DEFAULT only fills in omitted columns and NOT NULL rejects the explicit null
The column stores an empty string
The column stores null, because an explicit value always wins
quiz.explain: `DEFAULT` applies when a column is absent from the statement, not when it is present and null. An explicit null is a value, and `NOT NULL` refuses it. This is a common source of "but I set a default" confusion.

quiz.q: You want at most one row per user in a nullable `referral_code` column. Is `referral_code text UNIQUE` enough?
options: Yes, UNIQUE guarantees at most one row per value including null
No, because UNIQUE allows many null rows since two unknown values are not considered equal
Yes, but only if the column is also indexed
No, because UNIQUE only works on primary keys
quiz.explain: `NULL` means unknown, and Postgres will not claim two unknowns are duplicates, so a nullable unique column can hold unlimited nulls. If null must be excluded, add `NOT NULL` or use a partial unique index with a `WHERE ... IS NOT NULL` clause.

## The problem

The task list screen shows a small coloured chip with the category name next to each task. You wrote the endpoint yourself: select the tasks, join the categories, return one flat array. It shipped, and it worked, and two days later a user writes in to say half her tasks vanished from the list.

They did not vanish. They were the uncategorized ones. Your query said `INNER JOIN categories`, and an inner join is a filter: it returns only rows that found a match. Every task with a null `category_id` had no category to match, so the database quietly removed it from the result. There was no error, no crash, no log line, and a 200 response. One word (`LEFT`) was the difference between a list and a filtered list, and the default is the filtered one.

## The idea

Every relationship in a database is a screen you have already built.

A user has many tasks. That is your task list screen, and it is called **1:N**: the "many" side stores the reference. A task can carry several tags and a tag can appear on many tasks. That is your filter chips row, and it is called **M:N**: neither side can store the reference, so a third table exists purely to hold pairs. A user has one profile. That is your settings screen, and it is 1:1, which is rare and usually means two tables that wanted to be one.

The mechanism is the **foreign key**, and the analogy is a navigation param. When you push a screen with `{ taskId }`, the screen assumes that task exists, and when it does not you get a blank screen and a bug report. A foreign key is the database refusing to let the reference be wrong in the first place: you cannot insert a task pointing at a category id that is not there, and you cannot delete a category out from under a task without saying what happens to the task.

## In practice

The declaration is two extra words on a column.

```sql
CREATE TABLE tasks (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES auth.users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  category_id uuid REFERENCES categories(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  title       text NOT NULL,
  due_date    date,
  is_completed boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false
);
```

Notice `user_id` is `NOT NULL` and `category_id` is not. A task without an owner is meaningless. A task without a category is normal. That single difference is what created the bug at the top of this module.

Now the join that actually renders the screen:

```sql
SELECT t.id, t.title, t.due_date, c.name AS category_name, c.color
FROM tasks t
LEFT JOIN categories c ON c.id = t.category_id
WHERE t.user_id = $1
ORDER BY t.due_date ASC NULLS LAST
LIMIT 20;
```

`LEFT JOIN` means "keep every row on the left, fill the right side with nulls when there is no match". `INNER JOIN` means "keep only matched pairs". Read them as *keep everything* versus *keep intersections*, and pick deliberately every single time.

Many-to-many needs a join table, and its primary key should be the pair:

```sql
CREATE TABLE task_tags (
  task_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tasks(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  tag_id  uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tags(id)  ON DELETE CASCADE,
  PRIMARY KEY (task_id, tag_id)
);
```

A composite primary key gives you uniqueness for free: the same tag cannot be attached to the same task twice, so your "add tag" endpoint cannot create duplicates no matter how many times the user taps.

Aggregation is how you render counts and badges. `GROUP BY` collapses rows into buckets, and the aggregate functions summarise each bucket.

```sql
SELECT c.name,
       COUNT(t.id) AS task_count,
       COUNT(t.id) FILTER (WHERE t.is_completed) AS done_count
FROM categories c
LEFT JOIN tasks t ON t.category_id = c.id AND t.user_id = $1
WHERE c.user_id = $1
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY task_count DESC;
```

Two subtleties are doing real work there. `COUNT(t.id)` not `COUNT(*)`, because a left join pads unmatched rows with nulls and `COUNT(*)` counts that padding as one, so an empty category would report a count of 1. And the `t.user_id = $1` condition sits in the `ON` clause, not the `WHERE`. Put it in `WHERE` and you filter out the null-padded rows after the join, which turns your `LEFT JOIN` back into an inner join and drops every empty category.

Finally, `ON DELETE` is a product decision that happens to be written in DDL:

| Choice | What the user experiences |
|---|---|
| `CASCADE` | Delete the user, their tasks go with them. Correct for "delete my account". |
| `SET NULL` | Delete a category, the tasks survive as uncategorized. Correct for a label. |
| `RESTRICT` | You cannot delete a category that still has tasks. Correct when the app should force a choice first. |

Before you type one of those, answer the question in product terms: after this delete, what should the user see on their screen? Then write the clause that produces that.

## In your world

Day 12 gives you the 1:N case in `task-manager-api` (user to tasks, category to tasks). `chat-app-api` is where M:N stops being theory: a conversation has many participants and a user is in many conversations, so a participants table with a composite key holds the whole model. `file-vault-api` adds the weird one, a self-referential foreign key where `parent_folder_id` points back at the same table, which is a tree and is why recursive queries exist.

Your work backend's feed is a pile of these joins under load. When a feed query joins four tables and the shape looks right but the numbers are subtly off, the first thing to check is whether an inner join is silently filtering, and the second is whether a condition on an outer table drifted into the `WHERE`.

## Watch out

- `JOIN` with no qualifier means `INNER JOIN`. The default is the destructive one.
- A condition on the right-hand table of a `LEFT JOIN` belongs in `ON`. In `WHERE` it cancels the outerness.
- `COUNT(*)` counts rows including null-padded ones. `COUNT(column)` skips nulls. With outer joins those differ by exactly the bug you are hunting.
- Every non-aggregated column in the select list must appear in `GROUP BY`. Postgres will refuse rather than guess, which is a kindness.
- `ORDER BY` on a nullable column: decide `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` yourself, because the default depends on sort direction and "no due date" showing up first is a design choice, not an accident.
tasks: In your scratch database create `categories`, `tasks`, `tags`, and `task_tags` with the foreign keys above, then insert three tasks where one has a null `category_id`.
Run the same select twice, once with `INNER JOIN` and once with `LEFT JOIN`, and confirm the row count differs by exactly the uncategorized task.
Try to insert a task whose `category_id` is a random UUID and read the foreign key violation message. Then map that message to the HTTP status you would return.
Delete a category and confirm the tasks survive with a null `category_id`. Then change the constraint to `ON DELETE CASCADE`, redo it, and watch the tasks disappear.
Write the per-category counts query, then break it on purpose by moving `t.user_id = $1` from the `ON` clause into `WHERE`, and explain out loud why the empty categories disappeared.
Attach the same tag to the same task twice and confirm the composite primary key rejects the second attempt.

quiz.q: Your task list joins categories and half the tasks are missing from the response. What is the most likely cause?
options: The categories table is missing an index
An `INNER JOIN` is dropping tasks whose `category_id` is null
`LIMIT` is being applied before the join
The foreign key is missing so the join cannot resolve
quiz.explain: An inner join returns only matched pairs, so any task with a null `category_id` has nothing to match and is excluded. `LEFT JOIN` keeps the left-hand rows and fills the category columns with nulls.

quiz.q: `FROM categories c LEFT JOIN tasks t ON t.category_id = c.id WHERE t.is_completed = false` returns no empty categories. Why?
options: Empty categories have no tasks so they were never in the join result
The `WHERE` clause runs after the join and discards the null-padded rows, making the left join behave like an inner join
`is_completed` needs to be compared with `IS FALSE` on nullable columns
`LEFT JOIN` only preserves rows when the right table is empty overall
quiz.explain: The left join produces a row for the empty category with all task columns null, then the `WHERE` tests `null = false`, which is not true, so the row is filtered out. Move the condition into the `ON` clause to keep the outer behaviour.

quiz.q: You need per-category task counts and empty categories must show zero. Which count expression is correct?
options: `COUNT(*)`, because it counts every row in each group
`COUNT(t.id)`, because it ignores the null-padded rows a left join produces
`SUM(1)`, because it is equivalent and clearer
`COUNT(DISTINCT c.id)`, because it deduplicates the group
quiz.explain: With a left join, an empty category still produces one row where all task columns are null. `COUNT(*)` counts that row as 1; `COUNT(t.id)` skips nulls and correctly reports 0.

quiz.q: A `projects` table is referenced by `issues`. Product says deleting a project must not be possible while issues remain. Which foreign key behaviour matches?
options: `ON DELETE CASCADE`
`ON DELETE SET NULL`
`ON DELETE RESTRICT`
No clause is needed; deletes are blocked by default in Postgres for any referenced row
quiz.explain: `RESTRICT` refuses the delete while children exist, which pushes the decision back to the product (archive it, move the issues, or delete them explicitly). `NO ACTION` is the actual default and behaves similarly but defers the check to the end of the statement.

m1-3.content:
## The problem

The "Due this week" tab was instant for six months. Then a power user with 100,000 tasks opens it and the pull-to-refresh spinner sits there for four seconds. Nothing changed in the app. Nothing changed in the query. Your dev database has 100 rows and is still instant, which is why this is going to reach production.

The same week, a different bug: a user drags a task into a category, the task moves, and the category's counter does not. Two writes, one landed, the request died between them, and the database now holds a state your product does not allow. Same lesson from two directions: the database has machinery for making reads fast and for making multi-step writes all-or-nothing, and skipping it gets you four-second screens and impossible data.

## The idea

An index is the index at the back of a book. Without one, finding every mention of "transactions" means reading all 600 pages. With one, you flip to the T section, read a line, and jump straight to page 412. The cost is that the index took pages to print and must be reprinted whenever the book changes.

Postgres's default index is a **B-tree**: a sorted, shallow, wide tree. "Shallow" is the part that matters. At a million rows the tree is roughly four levels deep, so a lookup is about four page reads instead of a million row reads. That is the entire performance story, and it is why the fix for a four-second screen is usually one line of DDL rather than a rewrite.

A **transaction** is the other half. It is `Promise.all` for writes, except the guarantee runs the other way: not "all of them started" but "either all of them are visible or none of them ever happened". Between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`, nobody else sees your half-finished work, and if anything throws, `ROLLBACK` erases it as if the statements were never run.

## In practice

Start by asking the database what it is doing. `EXPLAIN` shows the plan; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and shows the plan with real timings.

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, title, due_date
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 'a1b2...'
  AND due_date BETWEEN '2026-08-10' AND '2026-08-17'
ORDER BY due_date;
```

Before any index you will see two words that explain the four seconds:

```
Sort  (cost=... rows=37)
  ->  Seq Scan on tasks  (rows=100000)
        Filter: ((user_id = 'a1b2...') AND ...)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 99963
```

**Seq Scan** means it read every row. **Rows Removed by Filter: 99963** means it threw away 99.96% of that work. Then the `Sort` sorted the survivors in memory. Add the index:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_tasks_user_due ON tasks (user_id, due_date);
```

and the plan becomes an **Index Scan** with no separate `Sort` step, because the index is already stored in `(user_id, due_date)` order and Postgres can walk it in that order.

Column order in a composite index is not cosmetic. Think of a phone book sorted by last name then first name. It answers "all the Rajs", and "all the Rajs, alphabetical by first name", instantly. It is useless for "everyone named Aswin", because that requires scanning every last name. This is the **leftmost prefix rule**: an index on `(a, b)` serves `WHERE a`, `WHERE a AND b`, and `WHERE a ORDER BY b`. It does nothing for `WHERE b` alone.

Indexes are not free, so you do not add them everywhere. Each one is a second structure that must be updated on every write to its columns, and it consumes disk. The rule is narrow: index your foreign keys, and index the exact combination your real queries filter and sort by.

Now the write side. Two statements that must both happen go inside one transaction.

```sql
BEGIN;

UPDATE tasks    SET category_id = 'work-uuid' WHERE id = 'task-uuid';
UPDATE categories SET task_count = task_count + 1 WHERE id = 'work-uuid';

COMMIT;
```

If the second statement fails, `ROLLBACK` (or a crashed connection, which rolls back automatically) undoes the first. That is **Atomicity**: all or nothing. **Consistency**: constraints are checked, so a transaction cannot commit a state the schema forbids. **Isolation**: concurrent transactions do not see each other's uncommitted work. **Durability**: once `COMMIT` returns, the data survives a power loss.

Isolation is enforced partly by **locks**. When you `UPDATE` a row, your transaction holds a lock on it until the transaction ends, and another transaction wanting that row waits. Usually the wait is microseconds. It becomes visible in two ways: a transaction left open while your code awaits something slow holds its locks the whole time and blocks real users, and two transactions that lock the same two rows in opposite order deadlock, at which point Postgres kills one with an error. The fix for the second is boring and reliable: always touch rows in a consistent order.

## In your world

The `task-manager-api` migration you write on day 12 has three indexes, and you can now justify each rather than copying it: `user_id` because it is a foreign key every query filters on, `category_id` for the same reason, and the composite `(user_id, due_date)` because "my tasks, soonest first" is the screen. On day 21 the transaction half of this module becomes `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and the question of why two buyers cannot both get the last item.

One trap specific to your stack: `supabase-js` sends each call as its own HTTP request through PostgREST, so you cannot wrap two of its calls in a transaction. There is no `BEGIN` to send. When you truly need atomicity there you push both statements into a Postgres function and call that once, or you connect with a Postgres driver directly. Your work backend takes the second route, which is why its query layer can express a real transaction and your practice projects mostly cannot.

## Watch out

- `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually executes the statement, so on an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` it really writes. Wrap it in `BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;` when you need the plan for a write.
- A sequential scan is not always wrong. On a small or mostly-returned table, reading everything is cheaper than bouncing through an index, and Postgres knows it. Judge by timing, not by the word "Seq".
- A plain index on a boolean rarely helps, because half the table matches. You usually want a partial index: `CREATE INDEX ... ON tasks (user_id) WHERE is_completed = false`.
- Your dev database is not a performance test. Seed 100k rows before you believe a query is fast.
- Long transactions are the quiet killer. Open, write, commit. Never hold one across an `await` on a network call.
tasks: Seed 100,000 rows into your scratch `tasks` table with `INSERT INTO tasks (user_id, title, due_date) SELECT ..., 'task ' || g, current_date + (g % 365) FROM generate_series(1, 100000) g;`
Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the due-date-range query before adding any index, and write down the node type, the total time, and the "Rows Removed by Filter" number.
Create the composite index on `(user_id, due_date)`, run the identical `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, and record the new node type and time. Compute the speedup.
Prove the leftmost prefix rule: query `WHERE due_date = '2026-09-01'` with no `user_id` filter and confirm from the plan that your composite index is not used.

Open two psql sessions. In session one run `BEGIN; UPDATE tasks SET title = 'a' WHERE id = X;` without committing. In session two update the same row and watch it block. Then `ROLLBACK` in session one and watch session two proceed.
Run a two-statement transaction, deliberately make the second statement fail (violate a CHECK), then `ROLLBACK` and confirm with a `SELECT` that the first statement left nothing behind.

quiz.q: An index exists on `tasks (user_id, due_date)`. Which query can it NOT help?
options: `WHERE user_id = $1`
`WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY due_date`
`WHERE due_date BETWEEN $1 AND $2`
`WHERE user_id = $1 AND due_date > $2`
quiz.explain: A B-tree is sorted by the leftmost column first, so it can only be traversed usefully when the query constrains that leading column. Filtering on `due_date` alone would require scanning every `user_id` section of the index, which is no better than scanning the table.

quiz.q: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on a `SELECT` shows `Seq Scan` with `Rows Removed by Filter: 99963`. What does that number tell you?
options: 99,963 rows were locked during the scan
Postgres read those rows and discarded them, which is wasted work an index could avoid
The query returned 99,963 rows
99,963 rows failed a constraint check
quiz.explain: It is the count of rows the executor touched and threw away. A high ratio of removed rows to returned rows is the clearest signal that the filter columns want an index.

quiz.q: Why is adding an index to every column a bad default?
options: Postgres allows a maximum of four indexes per table
Indexes only work on primary keys
Each index must be maintained on every write and consumes disk, so unused indexes slow down inserts and updates for no read benefit
Multiple indexes on one table confuse the planner into always choosing a sequential scan
quiz.explain: An index is a second data structure kept in sync with the table. Reads that use it get faster; every write pays for it. Index the foreign keys and the actual filter/sort combinations your queries use.

quiz.q: A request transfers a task between categories with two UPDATEs and crashes between them. Wrapping both in `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` prevents the half-applied state because of which ACID property?
options: Isolation
Atomicity
Durability
Consistency
quiz.explain: Atomicity means the transaction is an indivisible unit: either every statement is visible after commit, or none of them ever happened. A dropped connection rolls the transaction back automatically.

quiz.q: Why should you never hold a transaction open across an `await` on an external HTTP call?
options: Postgres closes idle transactions after 100ms
The transaction holds row locks for the entire duration of the network call, blocking other users' writes
HTTP calls cannot be made while a transaction is open
The connection pool converts it into an autocommit statement
quiz.explain: Locks are held until the transaction ends. If a payment provider takes two seconds to respond, every other transaction wanting those rows waits two seconds. Do the external call outside the transaction, then open, write, and commit quickly.

trap.title: Make the screen slow on purpose
trap.content:
Do not read about the four-second screen. Produce it.

1. Seed 200,000 tasks for a single `user_id` with `generate_series`, spreading `due_date` across a year.
2. Drop every index on the table except the primary key: `DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_tasks_user_due;`
3. Time the real screen query with `\timing on` in psql, running it five times so the cache is warm. Record the median.
4. Now add the composite index and run the identical query five more times. Record the median again.

You should see something between a 50x and a 500x difference. Write down both numbers and the two plan node types (`Seq Scan` versus `Index Scan`) somewhere you will find later.

The point is not the number. The point is that this table was fast yesterday, the code did not change, and nothing in your test suite would have caught it, because your test database has 100 rows. From now on, when a screen is slow in production and fine in dev, your first move is `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` against production-sized data, not a rewrite of the endpoint.

m1-4.content:
## The problem

A team ships fast by clicking. New column? Table editor. New policy? Toggle in the dashboard. It works for four months. Then three things happen in one week.

A new developer joins and asks how to get a working local database. The honest answer is "screenshot the table editor and recreate it by hand", and two days later he has something nearly but not exactly the same. Then the team wants a staging environment and discovers nobody can reproduce the schema, only copy the production data. Then on a Friday someone renames a column in the dashboard because it was "obviously a typo", the mobile app starts returning 500s, and there is no diff to read, no pull request to revert, and no record of who did it. The database drifted away from the repository, and the repository is the only thing the team knows how to reason about.

## The idea

The first thing to get straight: **Supabase is not a database**. It is a real, ordinary PostgreSQL server with a set of services arranged around it, each one a normal program you could run yourself on a laptop.

Think of it the way you think of Expo. Expo is not a different React Native; it is React Native plus a curated set of native modules and a dashboard, and the moment you need to, you can drop to the underlying platform. Supabase is Postgres plus a curated set of services and a dashboard, and you can always drop to `psql`.

Here is what is actually running:

| Piece | What it really is |
|---|---|
| Database | A PostgreSQL instance. You get a connection string. `psql` works. Every index, trigger, and transaction from the last three modules applies unchanged. |
| PostgREST | A server that reads your schema and exposes tables, views, and functions as a REST API. `supabase-js` is a typed client for this, which is why its query builder looks so much like SQL. |
| Auth (GoTrue) | A signup/login server that writes users into an `auth.users` table **in that same database**, and issues JWTs. |
| Realtime | A server that tails the database's write-ahead log and pushes row changes to subscribed clients over WebSockets. |
| Storage | An object store for files, with its metadata in a `storage` schema in the same database. |
| Dashboard | A web UI in front of all of the above. Convenient. Not the source of truth. |

That "same database" detail is the key that unlocks a lot. Because `auth.users` is a real table in your database, you can point a foreign key at it: `user_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES auth.users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`. Deleting a user cascades to their tasks, enforced by Postgres, with no application code involved.

## In practice

Create a project at supabase.com, pick a region near your users, and save the database password somewhere real. Then find these four things in the dashboard and understand what each one is for.

**The SQL editor.** A `psql` prompt in a browser tab. This is where you run migrations by hand until you set up the CLI. It runs as a privileged role, which matters later in this module.

**The connection string.** Something shaped like `postgresql://postgres:PASSWORD@db.PROJECTREF.supabase.co:5432/postgres`. You can point `psql`, a migration tool, or a Postgres driver at it. There is also a pooled connection on a different port for serverless environments, which gets its own side quest later.

**The two keys.** This distinction is the most consequential thing in this module.

| Key | Where it belongs | RLS |
|---|---|---|
| anon / publishable | Shipped inside your React Native bundle. Public by design. | Fully enforced. Every query is filtered by your policies. |
| service_role / secret | Server-side environment variables only. | **Bypassed entirely.** |

Read that second row again. The service role key does not have generous permissions; it has *no* row-level restrictions at all. Every query it makes sees every row of every user. That is appropriate for a trusted server doing its own authorization, and catastrophic in a mobile bundle, a client env var, a committed `.env`, or a screenshot in a Slack thread. Anyone holding it can read and rewrite your entire database.

Your Task Manager will use that key, which means for the next three days *your code* is the only thing between one user and another user's data. Day 13 is where you feel how thin that is.

**Migrations, as a concept.** A migration is a timestamped SQL file that lives in `supabase/migrations/`, is committed to git, and is applied in order, once each. The consequence is what matters: your schema stops being "whatever state that one server happens to be in" and becomes a replayable history any environment can be built from. New developer? Run the migrations. Staging? Run the migrations. Bad change? Write a new migration that undoes it, because a migration that has run is a historical fact, not a draft you edit. The mechanics come tomorrow; today the shift is that schema changes are code, and code goes through review.

## In your world

In `task-manager-api` you will keep every schema change as a numbered file under `supabase/migrations/`, starting with `001_create_categories_and_tasks.sql`, and you will run each one by pasting it into the SQL editor. That is a fine way to start, and it already gives you the property that matters: the repository, not the dashboard, describes your database.

Your work backend enforces the grown-up version. Migration files are generated by a CLI command so timestamps always increase correctly, they are strictly append-only (editing one that has already run is how two environments quietly diverge), and merging to the main branch applies the pending ones to production as part of the deploy. A migration file there is not a note to yourself. It is a deploy artifact that runs against real user data, exactly once, unattended.

## Watch out

- Changes made by clicking in the dashboard leave no trace in git. If you must click, immediately write the equivalent SQL into a migration file so the next environment gets it too.
- The SQL editor runs with a privileged role that bypasses RLS. Testing "can user A see user B's rows?" in the SQL editor proves nothing at all. You need two real accounts and two real tokens.
- Do not add your own columns to `auth.users`. Create your own `profiles` table with a foreign key to it. Supabase owns that schema and will change it.
- Free-tier projects pause after a stretch of inactivity. If your API suddenly cannot connect after a quiet week, check the dashboard before you debug your code.
- `supabase-js` talks to PostgREST over HTTP, not to Postgres directly. That is why there is no transaction API on it, and why some things you can express in SQL need a database function instead.
tasks: Create a Supabase project, then connect to it from your terminal with `psql` using the connection string and run `select version();` to prove it is ordinary Postgres.
Run `\dn` in that psql session to list the schemas, and find `auth`, `storage`, and `public`. Then run `select id, email from auth.users limit 5;` after creating one test user via the dashboard.
Find both API keys in the project settings. Write a one-sentence note next to each saying exactly which file in your project may contain it and which must never.
In the SQL editor, create a throwaway table, enable RLS on it with no policies, insert a row, then select it. Explain why the select still returned the row.

Create a `supabase/migrations/` folder in `task-manager-api` and put a `000_notes.sql` file in it containing only comments describing your intended schema. Commit it. You now have a schema history with one entry.
Write down, in your own words and without looking, what PostgREST, GoTrue, and Realtime each do and which one your RN app talks to for a live chat screen.

quiz.q: What does the Supabase service_role (secret) key change about how your queries run?
options: It grants broader permissions but row-level security policies still apply
It bypasses row-level security entirely, so every query can see and modify every row
It only unlocks the Storage and Realtime services
It signs JWTs so `auth.uid()` resolves to the current user
quiz.explain: The service role is a trusted server-side identity that RLS does not restrict. That is why authorization must be handled in your own code when you use it, and why the key can never appear in a client bundle.

quiz.q: Why can a `tasks` table declare `user_id uuid REFERENCES auth.users(id)`?
options: Supabase syncs users into your public schema in the background
Because `auth.users` is a real table in the same Postgres database, so a normal foreign key works
Because PostgREST resolves the reference at query time
It cannot; foreign keys across schemas are not allowed in Postgres
quiz.explain: Auth is a service writing to a table in your own database, not an external system. That means ordinary Postgres features (foreign keys, cascading deletes, joins) work against it.

quiz.q: You test row-level security by running `select * from tasks;` in the Supabase SQL editor and you see every user's rows. What have you learned?
options: Your policies are broken and need fixing
RLS is disabled on the table
Nothing about your policies, because the SQL editor runs as a privileged role that bypasses RLS
The policies only apply to inserts and updates
quiz.explain: The SQL editor is not a user session. To test policies you need a client authenticated with a real user's access token, which is what makes `auth.uid()` resolve to that user.

quiz.q: What is the practical argument for migrations over changing the schema in the dashboard?
options: Migrations run faster than the table editor
The dashboard cannot express constraints or indexes
Migrations make the schema a reviewable, replayable history so any environment can be rebuilt and any change can be traced
Migrations are required before you can enable row-level security
quiz.explain: The dashboard mutates one server and leaves no record. A migration is code: it goes through review, lands in git with an author and a reason, and produces an identical schema in every environment that runs it.

sq-2.content:
## The problem

Every schema you inherit has a column somebody regrets. A `tags` column holding `'sql,postgres,backend'`. An `address3` that is always empty. A `price` stored as a float that sums to 19.989999999999998 on the invoice screen. None of these were stupid; each was the fastest thing to type that day, and each becomes a migration with a data backfill later.

## The idea

Normalization has a formal definition and a useful one. The useful one: **every fact lives in exactly one place**. 1NF: one value per cell, so no comma-separated lists and no `col1, col2, col3` repeating groups. 2NF: no column depends on only part of a composite key. 3NF: no non-key column is determined by another non-key column, so if `city` follows from `postcode`, `city` does not belong in that table.

Denormalizing on purpose is fine and often necessary: a cached counter, a copied `seller_id` to avoid a three-table join, a materialized view of stats. The rule that keeps it honest is that duplicating a fact makes you responsible for keeping the copies in sync, so name the mechanism (a trigger, a job, a scheduled refresh) before you ship the duplication.

## In practice

Three real designs. For each, write down what breaks before you read on, then write the DDL you would replace it with.

**Drill 1.** `posts (id uuid, title text, tags text)` where `tags` holds `'sql,postgres,backend'`. It cannot be indexed usefully, "all posts tagged sql" needs `LIKE '%sql%'` which also matches `nosql`, renaming a tag is a string rewrite across every row, and nothing stops `'sql,sql'`. Fix it with a `tags` table plus a `post_tags` join table keyed on `(post_id, tag_id)`. Only when tags are freeform and will never carry attributes of their own is `text[]` with a GIN index a defensible shortcut.

**Drill 2.** `users (id, email, address1, address2, address3)`. Repeating groups violate 1NF. A fourth address needs a schema change, you cannot mark one as default, and "users in Chennai" becomes three OR branches. Fix it with `addresses (id, user_id, line1, city, postcode, is_default boolean)` plus a partial unique index on `(user_id) WHERE is_default` for the one-default rule.

**Drill 3.** `payments (id, amount double precision, currency text)`. Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so sums drift and equality fails unpredictably. Free-text currency gives you `'USD'`, `'usd'`, and `'$'` in one column. Fix it with `amount_cents bigint NOT NULL CHECK (amount_cents > 0)` and `currency char(3) NOT NULL CHECK (currency ~ '^[A-Z]{3}$')`.

## In your world

Drill 3 is day 21 in `marketplace-api`, where cents stop being a style preference and become the reason a total is correct. Drill 1 returns in `file-vault-api` as JSONB metadata, where the judgement call is which attributes deserve real columns and which are genuinely open-ended. Drill 2 is the shape of nearly every "we need a second one of these" request you will ever get.

## Watch out

- 3NF is a default, not a law. Break it deliberately, in a commit message that says why.
- A comma-separated column is not just ugly, it is unqueryable and unconstrainable. That is the actual objection.
- `numeric` is exact and slower; integer cents are exact and fast. Either beats `float` for money.
tasks: Prove the float problem in psql: run `select 0.1::double precision + 0.2::double precision = 0.3;` and then `select 0.1::numeric + 0.2::numeric = 0.3::numeric;` and explain the two results.
Write the replacement DDL for all three drills, including the join table's composite primary key and the partial unique index for the default address.
Create the flawed `posts` table, insert a row tagged 'nosql', then run the `LIKE '%sql%'` query and watch it match. Fix the schema and rerun the equivalent join query correctly.
Take one table from any of your five practice projects and write down, for each column, which entity that fact belongs to. Flag anything that belongs somewhere else.
Pick one deliberate denormalization you can imagine needing (a task count per category) and write down the exact mechanism that would keep it in sync.

quiz.q: What is the strongest objection to storing tags as a comma-separated text column?
options: It wastes disk space compared to a join table
It cannot be indexed or constrained, so queries degrade to substring matching and duplicates cannot be prevented
Postgres has a 255-character limit on text columns
It violates 3NF specifically
quiz.explain: The problem is capability, not size. A list crammed into one cell cannot have a unique constraint, cannot have a foreign key, and cannot be searched without substring matching that produces false positives like 'nosql' matching 'sql'.

quiz.q: A `users` table has `address1`, `address2`, `address3`. Which normal form does this violate and what is the fix?
options: 3NF; move city into a lookup table
1NF; repeating groups belong in a separate `addresses` table with a foreign key back to the user
2NF; add a composite primary key
None; it is denormalized on purpose and therefore fine
quiz.explain: Repeating groups of the same attribute across numbered columns break first normal form. A child table with one row per address makes the count unbounded, lets you mark a default, and makes filtering by city a normal query.

quiz.q: You decide to store a denormalized `task_count` on each category. What must you commit to at the same time?
options: Adding an index on the counter column
A named mechanism that keeps the counter in sync with the tasks table, such as a trigger or a scheduled job
Dropping the tasks table's foreign key to categories
Recomputing the count on every read
quiz.explain: Duplicating a fact transfers responsibility for consistency from the database to you. Deliberate denormalization is fine; unowned denormalization becomes a number on a screen that nobody trusts.
